meta.titre: Thermal Decomposition: carbonates, hydroxides and nitrates

sections.contenu_markdown: A builder in Limbe heats limestone in a kiln to make quicklime for cement, and a baker heats baking soda in the oven so the cake rises. In both cases heat breaks a compound into simpler substances. This is called thermal decomposition. The products depend on the metal in the compound: compounds of very reactive metals, such as sodium and potassium, need much more heat to decompose than compounds of less reactive metals, such as copper. The GCE O/L paper tests this through the heating of carbonates, nitrates and hydroxides, and the equations and observations that go with them.

items: The reactivity series lists metals from the most reactive (potassium) to the least reactive (copper).
Oxygen relights a glowing splint, and a balanced equation has the same atoms on both sides.

sections.titre: Thermal decomposition of carbonates, hydroxides and nitrates
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Thermal decomposition** is the breakdown of a compound into simpler substances by heat. **The more reactive the metal, the more stable its compound is to heat.**

| Compound | Potassium and sodium (very reactive) | Magnesium, zinc, copper (less reactive) |
|---|---|---|
| Carbonate | no change in a Bunsen flame | metal oxide + carbon dioxide |
| Hydroxide | no change in a Bunsen flame | metal oxide + water |
| Nitrate | nitrite + oxygen | metal oxide + brown nitrogen dioxide + oxygen |

Calcium carbonate also decomposes to the oxide, but needs a stronger heat than copper carbonate.

General equations, with examples:

$$\mathrm{CuCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$$

$$\mathrm{Cu(OH)_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuO} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$$

$$2\mathrm{NaNO_{3}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaNO_{2}} + \mathrm{O_{2}}$$

$$2\mathrm{Cu(NO_{3})_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CuO} + 4\mathrm{NO_{2}} + \mathrm{O_{2}}$$

**Observations.** Copper(II) carbonate changes from green to black; copper(II) hydroxide from blue to black; copper(II) nitrate from blue crystals to a black solid with brown fumes. Zinc oxide is yellow when hot and white when cold. Sodium carbonate is not affected by heating in the laboratory.

variantes.nom: Lithium: the exception in Group I
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a Group I compound (especially lithium) is heated.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Lithium is in Group I but its compounds behave like those of magnesium in Group II. This similarity between a Group I element and a Group II element (diagonally placed) is called the **diagonal relationship**. Lithium carbonate decomposes: $\mathrm{Li_{2}CO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li_{2}O} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$, whereas sodium carbonate does not. Lithium nitrate gives the oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: $4\mathrm{LiNO_{3}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Li_{2}O} + 4\mathrm{NO_{2}} + \mathrm{O_{2}}$, whereas sodium nitrate gives only the nitrite and oxygen.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When baking soda or hard water is heated.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Hydrogencarbonates decompose easily, even those of sodium: $2\mathrm{NaHCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}} + \mathrm{H_{2}O} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$. This is why sodium hydrogencarbonate is used as baking powder: the carbon dioxide makes the cake rise.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives an observation and asks for a conclusion.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Brown fumes are nitrogen dioxide, which turns damp blue litmus paper red. Oxygen relights a glowing splint. Condensation on the cooler part of the tube shows that water is formed. Colour change of the residue (green or blue to black) suggests a copper compound.

sections.enonce_markdown: 12.4 g of green copper(II) carbonate, $\mathrm{CuCO_{3}}$, is heated strongly in a test tube until there is no further change. The gas is passed into limewater. (a) State what is seen in the tube and in the limewater. (b) Write the equation. (c) Calculate the mass of residue and the volume of gas formed at room temperature and pressure.

etapes.justification: Copper carbonate loses carbon dioxide and leaves a metal oxide.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The green solid turns **black** and the limewater turns **milky** because carbon dioxide is released.

etapes.justification: Carbonate of a less reactive metal gives oxide and carbon dioxide.

etapes.action: Convert the mass of carbonate to moles.

etapes.justification: The ratio $\mathrm{CuCO_3} : \mathrm{CO_2}$ is 1 : 1 and a gas occupies $24\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ per mole.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Heating gives $8.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of black copper(II) oxide and $2.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ of carbon dioxide; the mass lost is $4.4\ \mathrm{g}$, which is the mass of $0.100\ \mathrm{mol}$ of carbon dioxide.

items.erreur_markdown: "Sodium carbonate decomposes to sodium oxide and carbon dioxide, like all carbonates."
items.pourquoi_faux: Carbonates of very reactive metals (sodium, potassium) do not decompose with a Bunsen burner.
items.correction_markdown: Only carbonates of less reactive metals, and lithium carbonate, decompose to oxide + carbon dioxide.

items.erreur_markdown: "All nitrates give brown nitrogen dioxide when heated."
items.pourquoi_faux: Sodium and potassium nitrates only lose oxygen and form the nitrite. Brown fumes come from nitrates of less reactive metals.
items.correction_markdown: Sodium nitrate: $2\mathrm{NaNO_{3}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaNO_{2}} + \mathrm{O_{2}}$. Copper(II) nitrate gives brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide.

items.erreur_markdown: "Copper carbonate decomposes to copper metal and carbon dioxide."
items.pourquoi_faux: Heating a copper carbonate gives the metal oxide and carbon dioxide, not the free metal.

items.erreur_markdown: "Sodium nitrate behaves like lithium nitrate because both are Group I."
items.pourquoi_faux: Lithium is the exception: its nitrate and carbonate behave like those of magnesium (diagonal relationship).
items.correction_markdown: $4\mathrm{LiNO_{3}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Li_{2}O} + 4\mathrm{NO_{2}} + \mathrm{O_{2}}$ but sodium nitrate gives only the nitrite and oxygen.

items.pourquoi_faux: The atoms are not balanced: two nitrate groups give 2 N, so the equation must be balanced with 4 $\mathrm{NO_2}$ per 2 $\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2}$.

items.enonce_markdown:
Predict the result of strongly heating each of the following in a test tube. State any observation and write a balanced equation where a reaction occurs.

(a) Sodium carbonate, $\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}}$. (b) Zinc carbonate, $\mathrm{ZnCO_{3}}$. (c) Copper(II) hydroxide, $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_{2}}$. (d) Sodium nitrate, $\mathrm{NaNO_{3}}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **No change** with an ordinary Bunsen flame because sodium is very reactive.

(b) A solid that is yellow when hot and white when cold remains; carbon dioxide is given off (limewater turns milky): $\mathrm{ZnCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$

(c) The blue solid turns black and water condenses at the cool part of the tube: $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuO} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$

(d) The solid melts and oxygen is given off (a glowing splint relights); sodium nitrite remains: $2\mathrm{NaNO_{3}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaNO_{2}} + \mathrm{O_{2}}$

items.enonce_markdown: A blue crystalline solid is heated strongly. A brown gas is given off, a glowing splint relights near the mouth of the tube and a black solid remains. (a) Identify the solid and name the two gases. (b) Write the balanced equation. (c) Calculate the mass of black residue and the total volume of gas, at room temperature and pressure, from 18.8 g of the solid, taking it as copper(II) nitrate with no water of crystallisation.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The solid is copper(II) nitrate, $\mathrm{Cu(NO_{3})_{2}}$. The brown gas is **nitrogen dioxide** and the gas that relights the splint is **oxygen**. The black solid is copper(II) oxide.

(b) $2\mathrm{Cu(NO_{3})_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CuO} + 4\mathrm{NO_{2}} + \mathrm{O_{2}}$

(c) $M(\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2}) = 64 + 2 \times (14 + 48) = 188$, so $n = \dfrac{18.8}{188} = 0.100\ \mathrm{mol}$. Ratio $\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2} : \mathrm{CuO}$ is 1 : 1, so $m(\mathrm{CuO}) = 0.100 \times 80 = $ **8.0 g**. Moles of gas: $\mathrm{NO_2}$ is $2 \times 0.100 = 0.200\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ is $0.100 \div 2 = 0.050\ \mathrm{mol}$, a total of $0.250\ \mathrm{mol}$. Volume $= 0.250 \times 24 = $ **6.0 $\mathrm{dm^3}$**.

items.enonce_markdown: A sample of impure limestone of mass 12.5 g (the impurities do not decompose) is heated strongly until its mass becomes constant. The gas given off has a mass of 4.4 g. (a) Write the equation for the decomposition of calcium carbonate. (b) Calculate the volume of the gas at room temperature and pressure. (c) Calculate the percentage of calcium carbonate in the limestone. (d) Use the reactivity series to explain why sodium carbonate would not decompose under the same conditions.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$

(b) $n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = \dfrac{4.4}{44} = 0.100\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $V = 0.100 \times 24 = $ **2.4 $\mathrm{dm^3}$**.

(c) The ratio $\mathrm{CaCO_3} : \mathrm{CO_2}$ is 1 : 1, so $n(\mathrm{CaCO_3}) = 0.100\ \mathrm{mol}$. $M(\mathrm{CaCO_3}) = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100$, so $m = 10.0\ \mathrm{g}$. Percentage $= \dfrac{10.0}{12.5} \times 100 = $ **80 %**.

(d) Sodium is much higher in the reactivity series than calcium; the more reactive the metal, the more stable its carbonate, so sodium carbonate does not decompose at the temperature of a Bunsen flame.

items_markdown: Thermal decomposition breaks a compound into simpler substances when it is heated.
The more reactive the metal, the more stable its carbonate, hydroxide and nitrate: sodium and potassium carbonates and hydroxides are unchanged by a Bunsen flame.
Carbonates and hydroxides of less reactive metals give the metal oxide plus carbon dioxide or water.
Sodium and potassium nitrates give the nitrite and oxygen; nitrates of magnesium, zinc and copper give the oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen ($2 : 4 : 1$ in the balanced equation).
Lithium behaves like magnesium (diagonal relationship); hydrogencarbonates such as sodium hydrogencarbonate decompose easily.
